Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

Summary: This note covers Sam Altman's backing of the teen-founded Induced AI, Google's Pixel 8 hardware launch, Flexport's valuation and leadership changes, the SBF trial details, and various other tech industry developments including LinkedIn's AI tools and IronNet's collapse.

Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time.

Google held its annual hardware event to showcase updates on the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. ### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony on default search engine deals, historical attempts at iOS preinstallation, chat deletion policies, and potential case outcomes.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults is made with the consumer in mind, allowing Google to collect data to be the best search engine across devices. Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices to connect services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software.

Testimony revealed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones, and platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that Bing would have been competitive with Google had it made similar deals with Apple, stating he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search.

Regarding data privacy, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours. Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with a litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed a personnel matter unrelated to the hold.

In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case, expected to continue for several weeks, could result in outcomes similar to the 1990s Microsoft trial, requiring Google to change behavior, share APIs, ban exclusive deals with manufacturers, and turn over collected data to competitors. The DOJ notes Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, and a ruling may impact ongoing FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-search-dominance-data-collection-and-manipulation.md

Title: Google Search dominance, data collection, and manipulation allegations
Summary: Examines Google's competitive advantages through data scale and ubiquity, user behavior patterns, and controversies surrounding query manipulation and ad revenue optimization.

Google's market dominance is attributed to its scale, longevity, ubiquity, and unmatched user data collection, which includes searches, smart speaker interactions, clicks on results and ads, enabling personalized services. While switching search providers is temporarily inconvenient due to loss of familiarity, users frequently revert to Google, making it the top Bing query in 2021 despite Microsoft defaults. Kent Walker defended Google's preference as a result of being the best rather than default status, citing intense industry competition.

Controversies surround allegations that Google manipulates search queries for ad revenue. Megan Grey, former DuckDuckGo vice-president, claimed Google replaces neutral terms like 'children's clothing' with monetizable brands like 'NIKOLAI-brand kidswear,' though she admitted possibly misinterpreting evidence. Google denies pushing users toward monetizable subjects, stating that ad keyword matching is a separate, long-standing process from the meaning-matching systems used for organic results. Wired removed an article on this topic for not meeting standards, but its widespread sharing suggests public skepticism regarding privacy and data handling.

Search quality has improved significantly due to data volume growth from approximately 9 ZB in 2013 to 120 ZB in 2023, shifting from static websites to live information within apps. The US faces an uphill legal battle proving Google broke the law to achieve its current market status quo. Additionally, Bing has attempted to compete with generative AI chatbot features and layout overhauls, though functionality remains limited compared to Google's established ecosystem.
</notes>

Title: Tech news: Sam Altman backs teen startup, Google unveils Pixel 8, and more industry updates
Summary: This note covers Sam Altman's backing of the teen-founded Induced AI, Google's Pixel 8 hardware launch, Flexport's valuation and leadership changes, the SBF trial details, and various other tech industry developments including LinkedIn's AI tools and IronNet's collapse.

Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time.

Google held its annual hardware event to showcase updates on the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro highlights improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI-powered features as upgrades over the Pixel 7 Pro, though it notes an underutilized temperature sensor.

Flexport, a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup, is valued at $8 billion. Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive ousted as Flexport CEO just a year into the job, criticized the company's founder and board in a Monday post on X following CNBC reporting.

In the SBF trial, the prosecution argued Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud for wealth and power, while the defense claimed he acted in good faith and got over his head. Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' details Sam Bankman-Fried's attempt to buy off Donald Trump to prevent him from running for president again, details emerging during the Manhattan Federal Court trial. Jacquelyn and Alex discussed the SBF trial, noting Jacquelyn's presence at the Southern District of New York courthouse listening to Bankman-Fried's case.

LinkedIn launched AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool.

IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, collapsed after going public in August 2021, laying off staff and seeing its stock price decline despite raising over $400 million.

Esther Rodriguez-Villegas, a career academic turned founder of Acurable, explains how her company creates wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions like sleep apnea and epilepsy.

Elon Musk claimed X generated 100–200 million posts daily in September, while CEO Linda Yaccarino later stated the figure was 500 million posts per day.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.
</notes>

Title: Tech news: Sam Altman backs teen startup, Google unveils Pixel 8, and more industry updates
Summary: This note covers Sam Altman's backing of the teen-founded Induced AI, Google's Pixel 8 hardware launch, Flexport's valuation and leadership changes, the SBF trial details, and various other tech industry developments including LinkedIn's AI tools and IronNet's collapse.

Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time.

Google held its annual hardware event to showcase updates on the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro highlights improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI-powered features as upgrades over the Pixel 7 Pro, though it notes an underutilized temperature sensor.

Flexport, a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup, is valued at $8 billion. Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive ousted as Flexport CEO just a year into the job, criticized the company's founder and board in a Monday post on X following CNBC reporting.

LinkedIn launched AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.
</notes>

### tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, invoking the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. The suit alleges that Google and Alphabet engage in anticompetitive behavior by siphoning off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

The lawsuit specifically cites Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE), Bard AI chatbot, and the Knowledge Graph (launched in May 2012) as tools that worsen publisher harm by misappropriating content and shifting traffic away from news sites. By 2020, the Knowledge Graph contained 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, much of which was derived from content misappropriated from publishers' websites and open source databases. Additionally, Google's Featured Snippets technology, which algorithmically extracts answers from webpages, is cited as a factor shifting traffic away from publishers' websites.

The case cites concerns over changing AdSense rates and Google's destruction of chat messages, an issue previously raised in the Epic Games antitrust lawsuit which Epic won. The suit seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products, including Google's and rivals', and allowing publishers opting out of SGE to appear in search results. The U.S. lawsuit follows a Google agreement with the Canadian government to pay Canadian media $73.5 million annually, distributed by headcount, after Meta began blocking Canadian news in August. The case arrives alongside the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, referencing a 2020 DOJ civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising. Plus cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news, magazine, and digital publications, noting news sites were the third largest category of AI training data. Hausfeld law firm states Google's scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press.

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony on default search engine deals, historical attempts at iOS preinstallation, chat deletion policies, and potential case outcomes.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults is made with the consumer in mind, allowing Google to collect data to be the best search engine across devices. Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices to connect services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software.

Testimony revealed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones, and platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that Bing would have been competitive with Google had it made similar deals with Apple, stating he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search.

Regarding data privacy, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours. Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with a litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed a personnel matter unrelated to the hold.

In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case, expected to continue for several weeks, could result in outcomes similar to the 1990s Microsoft trial, requiring Google to change behavior, share APIs, ban exclusive deals with manufacturers, and turn over collected data to competitors. The DOJ notes Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, and a ruling may impact ongoing FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.
</notes>

Question: Does the Fortune article suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried was responsible for the alleged deceit behind FTX's success, while the TechCrunch article focuses on Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison's admission of guilt to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse?

<notes>
### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-trump-offer/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-and-ftx-collapse.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX collapse
Summary: SBF reportedly offered $5 billion to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential re-run, while facing trial for orchestrating the collapse of FTX after valuations fell sharply.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) faces trial at Manhattan Federal Court for orchestrating the collapse of FTX, a crypto exchange he founded, accused of one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. SBF pleaded not-guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" is set to debut on the first day of the trial. In an interview on 60 Minutes, Lewis described SBF as having gone from having nothing to having $22.5 billion, becoming the richest person in the world under 30. Lewis and SBF met more than 100 times over two years. SBF raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global.

FTX secured marketing deals with sports icons Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million) to lend legitimacy. Trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. SBF's political fundraising strategy involved meeting with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence. However, SBF reportedly offered $5 billion to Trump to cancel his presidential re-run bid.

The value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value, so when valuations fell, they fell very hard. SBF has been denied bail and is blamed by those who lost money in Alameda or FTX for causing a ripple effect of crypto woes. Ayelet Noff, CEO of Sliced Brand, criticized SBF for having no management experience, being over his head, and delaying crypto adoption by at least a year or two.
</notes>

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony on default search engine deals, historical attempts at iOS preinstallation, chat deletion policies, and potential case outcomes.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults is made with the consumer in mind, allowing Google to collect data to be the best search engine across devices. Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices to connect services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software.

Testimony revealed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones, and platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that Bing would have been competitive with Google had it made similar deals with Apple, stating he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search.

Regarding data privacy, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours. Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with a litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed a personnel matter unrelated to the hold.

In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case, expected to continue for several weeks, could result in outcomes similar to the 1990s Microsoft trial, requiring Google to change behavior, share APIs, ban exclusive deals with manufacturers, and turn over collected data to competitors. The DOJ notes Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, and a ruling may impact ongoing FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.
</notes>

Title: Tech news: Sam Altman backs teen startup, Google unveils Pixel 8, and more industry updates
Summary: This note covers Sam Altman's backing of the teen-founded Induced AI, Google's Pixel 8 hardware launch, Flexport's valuation and leadership changes, the SBF trial details, and various other tech industry developments including LinkedIn's AI tools and IronNet's collapse.

Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time.

Google held its annual hardware event to showcase updates on the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro highlights improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI-powered features as upgrades over the Pixel 7 Pro, though it notes an underutilized temperature sensor.

Flexport, a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup, is valued at $8 billion. Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive ousted as Flexport CEO just a year into the job, criticized the company's founder and board in a Monday post on X following CNBC reporting.

In the SBF trial, the prosecution argued Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud for wealth and power, while the defense claimed he acted in good faith and got over his head. Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' details Sam Bankman-Fried's attempt to buy off Donald Trump to prevent him from running for president again, details emerging during the Manhattan Federal Court trial. Jacquelyn and Alex discussed the SBF trial, noting Jacquelyn's presence at the Southern District of New York courthouse listening to Bankman-Fried's case.

LinkedIn launched AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool.

IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, collapsed after going public in August 2021, laying off staff and seeing its stock price decline despite raising over $400 million.

Esther Rodriguez-Villegas, a career academic turned founder of Acurable, explains how her company creates wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions like sleep apnea and epilepsy.

Elon Musk claimed X generated 100–200 million posts daily in September, while CEO Linda Yaccarino later stated the figure was 500 million posts per day.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-trump-offer/sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-and-ftx-collapse.md

Title: SBF's $5B offer to Trump and FTX collapse
Summary: SBF reportedly offered $5 billion to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential re-run, while facing trial for orchestrating the collapse of FTX after valuations fell sharply.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) faces trial at Manhattan Federal Court for orchestrating the collapse of FTX, a crypto exchange he founded, accused of one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. SBF pleaded not-guilty to seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" is set to debut on the first day of the trial. In an interview on 60 Minutes, Lewis described SBF as having gone from having nothing to having $22.5 billion, becoming the richest person in the world under 30. Lewis and SBF met more than 100 times over two years. SBF raised approximately $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from backers including Sequoia, Temasek, and Tiger Global.

FTX secured marketing deals with sports icons Tom Brady ($55 million) and Steph Curry ($35 million) to lend legitimacy. Trading volume climbed to $15 billion per day. Anna Wintour contacted SBF via Zoom to sponsor her Met Costume Ball. SBF's political fundraising strategy involved meeting with Mitch McConnell to fund Republican candidates offsetting Trump's influence. However, SBF reportedly offered $5 billion to Trump to cancel his presidential re-run bid.

The value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value, so when valuations fell, they fell very hard. SBF has been denied bail and is blamed by those who lost money in Alameda or FTX for causing a ripple effect of crypto woes. Ayelet Noff, CEO of Sliced Brand, criticized SBF for having no management experience, being over his head, and delaying crypto adoption by at least a year or two.
</notes>

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.
</notes>

Question: What company is at the center of concerns regarding both potential foul play in search practices reported by The Age and the anticompetitive siphoning of content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers as discussed by TechCrunch?

<notes>
### tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, invoking the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. The suit alleges that Google and Alphabet engage in anticompetitive behavior by siphoning off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

The lawsuit specifically cites Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE), Bard AI chatbot, and the Knowledge Graph (launched in May 2012) as tools that worsen publisher harm by misappropriating content and shifting traffic away from news sites. By 2020, the Knowledge Graph contained 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, much of which was derived from content misappropriated from publishers' websites and open source databases. Additionally, Google's Featured Snippets technology, which algorithmically extracts answers from webpages, is cited as a factor shifting traffic away from publishers' websites.

The case cites concerns over changing AdSense rates and Google's destruction of chat messages, an issue previously raised in the Epic Games antitrust lawsuit which Epic won. The suit seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products, including Google's and rivals', and allowing publishers opting out of SGE to appear in search results. The U.S. lawsuit follows a Google agreement with the Canadian government to pay Canadian media $73.5 million annually, distributed by headcount, after Meta began blocking Canadian news in August. The case arrives alongside the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, referencing a 2020 DOJ civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising. Plus cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news, magazine, and digital publications, noting news sites were the third largest category of AI training data. Hausfeld law firm states Google's scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press.

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony on default search engine deals, historical attempts at iOS preinstallation, chat deletion policies, and potential case outcomes.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults is made with the consumer in mind, allowing Google to collect data to be the best search engine across devices. Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices to connect services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software.

Testimony revealed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones, and platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that Bing would have been competitive with Google had it made similar deals with Apple, stating he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search.

Regarding data privacy, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours. Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with a litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed a personnel matter unrelated to the hold.

In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case, expected to continue for several weeks, could result in outcomes similar to the 1990s Microsoft trial, requiring Google to change behavior, share APIs, ban exclusive deals with manufacturers, and turn over collected data to competitors. The DOJ notes Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, and a ruling may impact ongoing FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-search-dominance-data-collection-and-manipulation.md

Title: Google Search dominance, data collection, and manipulation allegations
Summary: Examines Google's competitive advantages through data scale and ubiquity, user behavior patterns, and controversies surrounding query manipulation and ad revenue optimization.

Google's market dominance is attributed to its scale, longevity, ubiquity, and unmatched user data collection, which includes searches, smart speaker interactions, clicks on results and ads, enabling personalized services. While switching search providers is temporarily inconvenient due to loss of familiarity, users frequently revert to Google, making it the top Bing query in 2021 despite Microsoft defaults. Kent Walker defended Google's preference as a result of being the best rather than default status, citing intense industry competition.

Controversies surround allegations that Google manipulates search queries for ad revenue. Megan Grey, former DuckDuckGo vice-president, claimed Google replaces neutral terms like 'children's clothing' with monetizable brands like 'NIKOLAI-brand kidswear,' though she admitted possibly misinterpreting evidence. Google denies pushing users toward monetizable subjects, stating that ad keyword matching is a separate, long-standing process from the meaning-matching systems used for organic results. Wired removed an article on this topic for not meeting standards, but its widespread sharing suggests public skepticism regarding privacy and data handling.

Search quality has improved significantly due to data volume growth from approximately 9 ZB in 2013 to 120 ZB in 2023, shifting from static websites to live information within apps. The US faces an uphill legal battle proving Google broke the law to achieve its current market status quo. Additionally, Bing has attempted to compete with generative AI chatbot features and layout overhauls, though functionality remains limited compared to Google's established ecosystem.
</notes>

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. SBF resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.
</notes>

During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds; he faces up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing in January.

### tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet
Summary: Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC filed a class action lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet, invoking the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief. The suit alleges that Google and Alphabet engage in anticompetitive behavior by siphoning off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI and older technologies.

The lawsuit specifically cites Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE), Bard AI chatbot, and the Knowledge Graph (launched in May 2012) as tools that worsen publisher harm by misappropriating content and shifting traffic away from news sites. By 2020, the Knowledge Graph contained 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, much of which was derived from content misappropriated from publishers' websites and open source databases. Additionally, Google's Featured Snippets technology, which algorithmically extracts answers from webpages, is cited as a factor shifting traffic away from publishers' websites.

The case cites concerns over changing AdSense rates and Google's destruction of chat messages, an issue previously raised in the Epic Games antitrust lawsuit which Epic won. The suit seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training AI products, including Google's and rivals', and allowing publishers opting out of SGE to appear in search results. The U.S. lawsuit follows a Google agreement with the Canadian government to pay Canadian media $73.5 million annually, distributed by headcount, after Meta began blocking Canadian news in August. The case arrives alongside the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, referencing a 2020 DOJ civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising. Plus cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating Google's Bard AI was trained on news, magazine, and digital publications, noting news sites were the third largest category of AI training data. Hausfeld law firm states Google's scheme causes profound harm to competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press.

### tech-news/google-antitrust/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-testimony.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and testimony
Summary: Overview of Google's antitrust trial, including CEO testimony on default search engine deals, historical attempts at iOS preinstallation, chat deletion policies, and potential case outcomes.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the trial, defending tactics including deals to make Google the default search engine. He stated the decision to pay for defaults is made with the consumer in mind, allowing Google to collect data to be the best search engine across devices. Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on iOS devices to connect services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software.

Testimony revealed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones, and platforms, including Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that Bing would have been competitive with Google had it made similar deals with Apple, stating he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search.

Regarding data privacy, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours. Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with a litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed a personnel matter unrelated to the hold.

In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior. Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case, expected to continue for several weeks, could result in outcomes similar to the 1990s Microsoft trial, requiring Google to change behavior, share APIs, ban exclusive deals with manufacturers, and turn over collected data to competitors. The DOJ notes Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, and a ruling may impact ongoing FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.
</notes>

Summary: This note covers Sam Altman's backing of the teen-founded Induced AI, Google's Pixel 8 hardware launch, Flexport's valuation and leadership changes, the SBF trial details, and various other tech industry developments including LinkedIn's AI tools and IronNet's collapse.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. Sam Altman has backed Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/sam-bankman-fried-trial-opening-statements-and-witness.md

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Overview of the prosecution and defense opening statements in the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, including allegations of theft, the defense's 'good faith' argument, and initial witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals and code contributions.

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX, began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, characterized Bankman-Fried not as a 'crypto boy' genius but as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. Allegations included using Alameda Research (a crypto hedge fund he owned) and Caroline Ellison (CEO of Alameda and his girlfriend) as fronts to gain secret access to customer funds, directing employees to conceal money flows, forging financial documents, and lying to customers, lenders, and investors. The prosecution also noted his funded jet-setting lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets.

In contrast, the defense, led by Mark Cohen, argued that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone and presented him as a nerdy startup founder acting in 'good faith.' This narrative aimed to counter the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain' portrayal, noting that Bankman-Fried had spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison prior to the trial. The defense claimed Alameda was a successful hedge fund operating legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, rather than a Ponzi scheme.

Following the opening statements, the prosecution called witness Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified about attempting to withdraw nearly $100,000 on November 8, 2021, which he never succeeded in doing. The prosecution also called Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of Bankman-Fried, who testified that he had legal immunity due to concerns that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime.

### tech-news/bankman-fried-trial/ftx-collapse/sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md

Title: SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX
Summary: This note covers the timeline of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the founding and rapid growth of FTX and Alameda Research, the collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, and the legal proceedings including arrests, pleas, and charges.

Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history.
